write.desc: Compactness on the real line: the sequence view and the open-cover view, the Heine-Borel theorem that both mean closed and bounded, the nested compact set property, and why compactness is the hypothesis that turns local information into global information. These points form one textbook section that builds to a single equivalence theorem and its first uses.

points.name: Sequential compactness
points.what: The learner can state the definition (every sequence in K has a subsequence converging to a point of K), check it for simple sets such as finite sets and [0,1], and explain why the limit must lie in K itself.
outside: convergence of a sequence and its limit

points.name: Sequentially compact means closed and bounded
points.what: The learner can prove that a subset of R is sequentially compact exactly when it is closed and bounded: one direction uses Bolzano-Weierstrass and the sequence characterisation of closed sets, and the other builds a sequence with no convergent subsequence from unboundedness or from a missing limit point.
outside: a set is closed exactly when it contains the limits of its convergent sequences
every subsequence of a convergent sequence converges to the same limit
limit point of a set as the limit of a sequence from the set

points.name: Open covers and finite subcovers
points.what: The learner can say what an open cover of a set is and what a finite subcover is, write down covers of given sets as indexed families of open sets, and decide in simple examples whether a given cover has a finite subcover.
outside: unions of indexed families of sets

points.name: Compactness by open covers
points.what: The learner can state the open-cover definition of compactness (every open cover has a finite subcover), stressing that it must hold for every cover, and can prove directly that finite sets are compact in this sense.

points.name: Why (0,1) and R are not compact
points.what: The learner can prove in both views that (0,1) and R are not compact: 1/n has no subsequence converging in (0,1) and n has no convergent subsequence at all, while the covers (1/n, 1) and (-n, n) have no finite subcover, and can say in their own words which feature (a missing endpoint, unboundedness) causes each failure.
outside: Archimedean property of the real numbers

points.name: A closed interval [a,b] is compact
points.what: The learner can prove that every open cover of [a,b] has a finite subcover by repeated bisection: if no finite subcover existed, the halves would give nested closed intervals whose common point lies in one open set of the cover that already contains a whole small interval.
outside: an open set contains an epsilon-neighbourhood of each of its points

points.name: The Heine-Borel theorem
points.what: The learner can prove that for a subset K of R the three conditions closed and bounded, sequentially compact, and every open cover has a finite subcover are equivalent, using that a closed subset of [a,b] is covered by adding its open complement to a cover, and that a cover-compact set must be bounded (cover by (-n,n)) and closed (cover by the complements of shrinking closed neighbourhoods of a missing limit point).
outside: the complement of a closed set is open

points.name: Nested compact sets
points.what: The learner can prove that a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets has nonempty intersection, by choosing a point in each set and taking a convergent subsequence, and can show with (0, 1/n) and [n, infinity) that the result fails without compactness.
outside: a set is closed exactly when it contains the limits of its convergent sequences

points.name: Compactness turns local into global
points.what: The learner can explain and use the pattern behind compactness arguments: when a property holds on a neighbourhood of each point of a compact set, a finite subcover makes it hold on the whole set (for example a function bounded near each point of [a,b] is bounded on [a,b]), and can see why the same argument breaks on (0,1).
